title: Trafficking Survivors Relief Act
official_summary:
Trafficking Survivors Relief Act

This act establishes a process to vacate convictions and expunge arrest records for certain criminal offenses committed by victims of human trafficking that directly result from or relate to having been a trafficking victim.

It defines the offenses eligible to be vacated or expunged and sets forth procedures for filing a motion.

The Government Accountability Office must assess the impact of this process, including the number of human trafficking survivors who file motions to vacate convictions or expunge records.

Under the act, U.S. Attorneys' Offices must report to the Department of Justice (DOJ) on the number of motions to vacate convictions or expunge arrest records that are filed. Additionally, the DOJ must report to Congress on professional training received by U.S. Attorneys on indicators of human trafficking during the preceding 12-month period.

The act permits certain grants for legal representation to be used to seek post-conviction relief.

Finally, the act allows a defendant to establish, as a defense, that the offenses were committed under duress by demonstrating that he or she was a victim of human trafficking at the time of the offense.

summary.headline: New law lets human trafficking survivors ask federal courts to clear convictions and arrest records for crimes tied to being trafficked.
summary.what_it_does: The law sets up a process for trafficking survivors to ask a court to cancel (vacate) certain federal convictions or erase (expunge) arrest records when the offense directly resulted from or related to being trafficked. It also lets a person charged with a crime argue, as a defense, that they acted under duress because they were a trafficking victim at the time. Grants for legal help may now be used to seek this kind of relief after a conviction. The law also adds reporting and review requirements for federal prosecutors, the Justice Department, and the Government Accountability Office.

who_it_affects.group: Survivors of human trafficking with federal criminal records
who_it_affects.how: They can file a motion to have qualifying convictions vacated or arrest records expunged if the offense was tied to their trafficking.

who_it_affects.group: People facing federal criminal charges who were trafficking victims
who_it_affects.how: They can claim as a defense that they committed the offense under duress because they were being trafficked at the time.

who_it_affects.group: Legal aid providers that receive certain federal grants
who_it_affects.how: They may use grant money to represent trafficking survivors seeking post-conviction relief.

who_it_affects.group: U.S. Attorneys' Offices and the Justice Department
who_it_affects.how: Prosecutors must report how many motions are filed, and the Justice Department must report to Congress on prosecutors' training in spotting signs of trafficking.
It must study the impact of the new process, including how many survivors file motions.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted January 23, 2026; the summary does not give a separate start date.
